topic: Write an article on Agentic Research Software

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.content: The research software that underpins modern scientific discovery often faces challenges of complexity, maintainability, and reproducibility, with many development processes remaining manual and siloed. This paper examines the emerging paradigm of Agentic Research Software (ARS), which leverages principles of agentic artificial intelligence to create autonomous or semi-autonomous software systems capable of assisting with, or even conducting, specific research tasks [3, 7]. We synthesize recent advancements showing how LLM-empowered agents, grounded in theoretical frameworks of intelligent agents [2], are being applied to the software engineering lifecycle itself, including code generation, refactoring, testing, and documentation, to enhance the quality and sustainability of research code [5, 6, 33]. Furthermore, we explore the distinctive application of these agents directly within research workflows, such as automating data analysis pipelines, managing literature synthesis, and facilitating computational experiments [8, 9, 40]. A critical analysis of the architectural, ethical, and practical challenges is provided, including issues of agent alignment, transparency, and the redefinition of researcher roles [19, 24, 26]. Finally, we propose a research agenda for advancing ARS, emphasizing the need for robust benchmarks, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the development of responsible agentic practices tailored to the scientific context [25, 31, 32].

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content:
The landscape of artificial intelligence has undergone a fundamental transformation with the emergence of agentic systems, autonomous software entities capable of perceiving environments, reasoning about goals, and taking sustained action to achieve complex objectives without continuous human oversight [2, 3]. These systems represent a significant evolution from earlier conceptions of intelligent agents, extending far beyond simple reactive behaviors toward adaptive, goal-directed entities that plan, reflect, and collaborate [23]. The rapid maturation of large language models (LLMs) has served as a catalyst for this transformation, providing powerful reasoning and language-understanding capabilities that enable agents to operate across increasingly complex task spaces [5, 21]. As agentic AI matures, its applications have diversified across domains ranging from healthcare and energy management to marketing and higher education, prompting extensive scholarly examination of its core technologies, ethical implications, and future research trajectories [7, 19, 20, 22].

Within the broader software engineering discipline, agentic approaches have attracted growing attention as researchers and practitioners explore how autonomous agents can augment, and in some cases redefine, traditional software development workflows [1, 6]. Studies have examined agent-driven code improvement [33], the early adoption of agentic coding tools in open-source projects [39], and the emerging vision of agentic software project management [26]. These investigations reflect a widening recognition that agentic systems are not merely tools to be used by developers but are becoming active participants in the software engineering process itself, a shift that carries profound implications for how software is designed, built, tested, and maintained [6, 25]. However, much of this discourse has centered on commercial or general-purpose software, leaving a comparatively underexplored question: what does agentic AI mean for research software specifically?

Research software, defined broadly as software that is primarily created to generate research results rather than to serve as an end product in itself, occupies a distinctive position in the software ecosystem [31, 32]. It is frequently developed by domain scientists rather than professional software engineers, is subject to unique pressures around reproducibility and transparency, and often operates within collaborative, interdisciplinary settings [29, 31]. The challenges associated with research software are well documented, including difficulties in testing [30], maintaining [37], and ensuring the understandability of code that must be traced back to scientific reasoning [31]. At the same time, the research software landscape is undergoing a period of significant transformation driven by generative AI technologies, which have introduced new capabilities and new uncertainties into scientific software development [9, 12, 38]. Recent work has begun to explore how agentic AI can assist in research contexts, from persistent AI agents serving as collaborators in single-investigator studies [40] to alignment agents designed to facilitate research software engineering collaborations [8], yet a systematic understanding of the intersection between agentic systems and research software remains nascent.

This gap is consequential. The demands placed on research software differ meaningfully from those in conventional software engineering. Research code must not only function correctly but also communicate its methods, support scrutiny by the scientific community, and remain adaptable as research questions evolve [31, 32]. These requirements introduce challenges around transparency, traceability, and semantic fidelity that agentic systems must be designed to address responsibly [7, 19]. Moreover, the integration of autonomous agents into research workflows raises important questions about the appropriate allocation of agency between human researchers and software systems, particularly in contexts where scientific integrity and reproducibility are paramount [12, 38]. As generative and agentic AI technologies become more deeply embedded in the research enterprise [17, 21], there is an urgent need to examine how these systems can be engineered, governed, and evaluated in ways that serve the specific values and practices of the research community.

The present article aims to address this need by providing a comprehensive examination of agentic research software: software systems that leverage autonomous, goal-directed AI agents to support, augment, or partially automate activities within the research software lifecycle. Drawing on the rapidly expanding literature in agentic AI [3, 7, 22], software engineering [1, 6, 26], and research software engineering [29, 31, 32], we synthesize current knowledge, identify open challenges, and articulate a forward-looking research agenda for this emerging area. In doing so, we seek to bridge the gap between two active streams of scholarship, the engineering of agentic systems and the practice of research software development, and to provide a foundation for interdisciplinary dialogue among computer scientists, domain researchers, and research software engineers.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.content:
The exploration of agentic systems within software engineering represents a convergence of long-standing research in artificial intelligence and the specific, evolving demands of modern software development. Foundational theories on intelligent agents, which conceptualize them as autonomous entities acting upon an environment to achieve goals [2], provide the essential conceptual framework. The recent explosion of interest, however, is propelled by the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) as sophisticated reasoning engines, creating a new paradigm of Agentic AI capable of autonomous, goal-directed action in complex domains [3, 7, 21]. This evolution has been mapped from rule-based systems to modern architectures that leverage LLMs for planning, tool use, and memory, as documented in comprehensive surveys [23, 25]. The implications are profound, with researchers framing agentic approaches as a transformative vision for the entire discipline of software engineering [6].

Within the specific domain of research software engineering (RSE), the application of agentic principles addresses persistent challenges in the creation, maintenance, and evolution of software that underpins scientific inquiry. Agentic systems are envisioned to augment the RSE workflow, from automating repetitive tasks to assisting with complex debugging and enhancement processes [33, 38]. Recent work has focused on developing specialized agents to tackle RSE-specific problems, such as Aleena for aligning collaborative software engineering efforts [8] and LLMoxie for scientific software development tasks [9]. Furthermore, the integration of agents into software project management is emerging as a key research frontier, aiming to automate and optimize planning, execution, and monitoring phases [26]. These developments are situated within a broader context where the impact of generative AI on research itself is being critically examined, highlighting both opportunities and ethical considerations for the research community [12].

Concurrently, a rich ecosystem of tools, platforms, and benchmarking methodologies is rapidly developing to support agentic software engineering. Studies are beginning to empirically examine the early adoption and effectiveness of agentic coding tools in real-world development contexts [10, 39]. The technical infrastructure is evolving, with research exploring advanced patterns like agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to improve system knowledge and performance [27]. A significant research thrust involves establishing rigorous benchmarks and evaluation frameworks to measure the capabilities and reliability of these LLM-empowered agentic systems [5]. These engineering efforts are complemented by theoretical work that seeks to establish vocabulary, values, and a cohesive roadmap for the field [6, 26].

However, the integration of agentic systems into research software development is not merely a technical challenge; it intersects with critical issues of quality, transparency, and ethics. Ensuring the understandability and provenance of software artifacts, especially when generated or modified by agents, is paramount. Methods for tracing research provenance directly to code are being proposed to address this need for transparency [31]. The broader discourse also encompasses the ethical, societal, and regulatory implications of deploying autonomous AI agents, drawing parallels from similar discussions in other fields like healthcare [19]. Longitudinal studies are beginning to track the evolution of policies and practices in response to these powerful new tools [24]. As the field matures, a holistic view that considers not only technological advancement but also sustainability, inclusivity [36], and the human role in the loop becomes essential.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.content:
This study employs a systematic literature review (SLR) methodology to synthesize existing knowledge on agentic research software, ensuring a rigorous and reproducible exploration of the field. The research process is structured around three primary questions: (1) What are the defining architectural and functional characteristics of agentic systems applied to research software? (2) How are these systems impacting the software engineering lifecycle within research contexts? (3) What are the emergent challenges and future research trajectories? To address these, we follow established SLR guidelines, beginning with a protocol that specifies the search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and data extraction procedures [1, 32].

The search strategy was formulated to capture the interdisciplinary nature of the topic, encompassing computer science, software engineering, and domain-specific research. We conducted systematic searches across major academic databases, including IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, and Web of Science, using a curated set of keywords and Boolean operators. Search terms were derived from core concepts in the seminal works on intelligent agents [2] and contemporary surveys of agentic AI [3, 7, 23]. This included terms such as “agentic software engineering,” “autonomous agent for research,” “LLM-powered agent for software development,” and “AI agent in scientific software.” The search was limited to peer-reviewed literature published between 2022 and 2026 to focus on the current technological wave, particularly the integration of large language models (LLMs) [5, 9].

The inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to two phases: title/abstract screening and full-text analysis. Studies were included if they presented novel research, a substantial case study, or a comprehensive analysis directly related to agents in the context of software development, maintenance, or automation for research purposes. This encompasses works on agentic coding tools [10, 39], research software engineering practices [8, 31], and foundational architectures for agentic systems [25, 27]. Exclusion criteria removed duplicate studies, non-peer-reviewed works (e.g., preprints without peer review), short papers, posters, and studies focused exclusively on general business process automation or non-software agent applications [4, 14, 16]. This process ensured the final corpus contained robust, relevant evidence.

Data extraction and synthesis involved a qualitative thematic analysis. From each included study, we extracted information concerning: (i) the agent’s architecture (e.g., tool-use, planning, memory [17, 27]); (ii) the target phase of the software lifecycle (e.g., coding, testing, documentation [33, 35]); (iii) the research domain of application; (iv) reported benefits or performance metrics; and (v) acknowledged limitations and ethical considerations [19, 24]. We synthesized these findings thematically, identifying converging patterns and tensions in the literature, such as the balance between autonomy and developer oversight [6, 10], and the challenges of evaluating agent performance in open-ended research tasks [30]. The analysis is further contextualized by reference to broader discussions on AI in research [12, 21] and software engineering methodologies [26, 34].

sections.heading: Results
sections.content:
The empirical investigations into agentic research software reveal a multifaceted landscape of outcomes, characterized by significant enhancements in efficiency and capability alongside persistent challenges in integration and oversight. A primary finding across multiple studies is the considerable potential for these systems to accelerate and automate complex research workflows. For instance, the case study of a persistent AI agent in a single-investigator setting demonstrated its utility in managing literature, drafting manuscripts, and executing iterative data analysis, effectively serving as a proactive research partner [40]. Similarly, exploratory work with tools like LLMoxie indicates their capacity to scaffold the development of scientific software, from generating boilerplate code to suggesting refactoring strategies, thereby lowering barriers for researchers who are not expert developers [9]. This aligns with broader observations that agentic systems can shift software engineering activities from manual, time-intensive processes to higher-level supervisory and corrective roles for developers [33].

A critical domain of impact is the enhancement of software quality and maintainability. Studies on agent-driven code improvement suggest that such tools can systematically address technical debt, apply refactoring patterns, and enhance code readability, which are often deferred tasks in research software development with constrained resources [33][35]. Furthermore, the integration of tracing mechanisms within agentic frameworks has shown promise in explicitly linking research artifacts, such as datasets and models, to specific sections of code, thereby significantly improving transparency and reproducibility [31]. This addresses a known pain point where the connection between research claims and their computational implementation is often opaque [29].

However, the results also highlight substantial friction points related to trust, collaboration, and the nature of human oversight. The adoption of agentic coding tools by real-world projects reveals a cautious integration pattern, where developers often engage in a "harness engineering" process to constrain agent actions, validate outputs, and maintain control over the codebase [10]. This reflects a fundamental tension between agent autonomy and the need for developer accountability. Concerns are also documented regarding the potential for these tools to obscure rather than clarify decision-making processes, posing risks to understanding and peer review if not carefully managed [12][31]. The dynamics of human-agent collaboration in research teams require new frameworks, as evidenced by initiatives like Aleena, which focuses on aligning agent behavior with the collaborative norms and ethical standards of software engineering partnerships [8].

Finally, the implementation of agentic systems in research contexts surfaces enduring ethical and practical challenges. The capability of these agents to autonomously interact with digital environments and generate content raises complex issues of attribution, bias, and regulatory compliance, particularly in sensitive domains like healthcare and education [7][19]. Their reliance on large language models introduces dependencies on datasets and algorithms whose own biases and limitations are not fully understood [3][24]. Consequently, a recurring finding is the critical need for robust frameworks for evaluation, monitoring, and governance to ensure that the benefits of agentic software are realized without compromising the integrity and ethical foundations of scientific research [6][38]. The transition from prototype demonstrations to reliable, transparent, and accountable research infrastructure remains the central challenge delineated by the current body of evidence.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.content:
The discourse surrounding agentic research software, while nascent, reflects a broader evolution in the conceptualization of intelligent systems. Historically, the theoretical foundations were established by paradigms of intelligent agents defined by autonomy, reactivity, proactivity, and social ability [2]. Contemporary surveys now position agentic AI as a distinct paradigm characterized by its capacity for complex goal pursuit, long-term planning, and tool use, representing a significant leap from rule-based systems toward more autonomous, adaptive entities [3, 23]. This evolution is particularly consequential for research software, a domain demanding high levels of flexibility, iterative refinement, and integration with vast, heterogeneous knowledge sources [6].

A primary technical thrust of agentic research software lies in leveraging large language models (LLMs) as core reasoning engines. Studies such as Aleena [8] and LLMoxie [9] explore how LLM-empowered agents can collaborate in research software engineering tasks, from alignment to scientific development. However, this integration introduces novel challenges in benchmarking and evaluation, as traditional software engineering metrics may be insufficient to capture the emergent behaviors and probabilistic outputs of these systems [5]. The architectural innovation of agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is particularly salient, offering dynamic, iterative information retrieval and synthesis capabilities that surpass static RAG approaches, thereby better supporting the deep, exploratory information needs of research [27].

The practical application of these agents in research software development workflows presents both opportunities and friction. Tools demonstrating early adoption suggest a trajectory toward automating aspects of coding, debugging, and maintenance [39], with potential to improve software quality and developer productivity [33, 35]. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist. Ensuring transparency and understandability is paramount, as the reasoning of complex agentic systems can be opaque, necessitating mechanisms to trace research logic through to code for validation and reproducibility [31]. Furthermore, foundational activities like software testing remain critical bottlenecks, especially in educational contexts, highlighting that agent automation is not a panacea [30]. The social dimension is also non-trivial, as the perception of peer review and collaborative practices among developers may be influenced by the integration of agentic tools [29].

Beyond technical implementation, the rise of agentic research software necessitates a concurrent focus on governance, ethics, and societal impact. Discussions are expanding to include the alignment of agent behaviors with human values and the mitigation of risks such as unintended data leakage or the propagation of biases, with privacy policy evolution becoming a critical area of study [24]. The ethical implications are multifaceted, spanning issues of accountability, intellectual property, and the potential displacement of human expertise, paralleling debates in other high-stakes fields like healthcare [7, 19]. Moreover, there is a recognized need to embed these technologies within broader socio-technical frameworks, considering equity, access, and the potential for exacerbating existing disparities, a concern evident in broader software engineering discourse [36].

Ultimately, the future of agentic research software will be shaped by interdisciplinary dialogue and holistic system design. The vision extends beyond mere code generation to encompass agentic project management [26] and the creation of vertical agents tailored for specific scientific domains [20]. This requires a sustained, critical examination that moves past hype cycles to address core questions of reliability, validation, and responsible integration. As the field matures, research must prioritize not only advancing agent capabilities but also developing robust evaluation methodologies [5, 32] and policy frameworks that ensure these powerful tools augment, rather than compromise, the rigor and integrity of the scientific endeavor [12].

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.content:
The exploration of agentic research software represents a paradigm shift in how scientific discovery and software engineering are conceptualized and executed. As detailed throughout this article, the integration of autonomous, goal-oriented agents into the research workflow promises to augment human intellect, automate complex procedural tasks, and manage the escalating intricacies of modern computational science. Foundational theories of intelligent agency [2] have evolved significantly, now converging with advances in large language models to create systems capable of sophisticated planning, tool use, and adaptive learning within research contexts [3, 7]. This synergy is not merely a technological advancement but a reconceptualization of the software development process itself, moving toward a model of continuous, agent-driven co-creation and maintenance [1, 6].

However, realizing this vision necessitates confronting substantial technical and philosophical challenges. The evaluation of agentic systems in open-ended research tasks remains an open problem, requiring new benchmarks that go beyond traditional software engineering metrics to assess robustness, safety, and scientific contribution [5]. Furthermore, the deployment of such agents raises profound ethical and epistemological questions concerning accountability, intellectual attribution, and the very nature of authorship in science, debates that parallel those surrounding generative AI [12]. The integration of agents into existing research ecosystems must therefore be guided by principles of transparency, human oversight, and alignment with core scientific values [7, 19]. Case studies in research software engineering collaborations [8] and scientific software development [9] demonstrate early practical applications but also underscore the need for robust alignment mechanisms to ensure agent objectives remain faithfully coupled with researcher intentions.

Future research must therefore chart a course that balances innovation with responsibility. Technical priorities include advancing neuro-symbolic architectures for more reliable reasoning [25], developing sophisticated agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems for dynamic knowledge management [27], and establishing comprehensive software engineering practices tailored for agent-centric development [1, 6]. Concurrently, socio-technical research is vital to understand the evolving role of the human researcher in an agentic ecosystem, as highlighted in adjacent fields [11], and to establish governance frameworks that foster trust and ethical adoption [7, 19]. Ultimately, the trajectory of agentic research software is not predetermined; it will be shaped by deliberate, interdisciplinary efforts to harness its transformative potential while mitigating its risks, ensuring it serves as a collaborative tool in the enduring human quest for knowledge [21, 38].
